title: Dosa
detailDescription: Dosa is a thin, crispy South Indian crepe made from a fermented batter of rice and black gram (urad dal), enjoyed hot with chutneys and sambar.
details: Origin & Popularity: Dosa originated in South India and has been a staple for centuries. Today, it’s enjoyed across India and internationally as a breakfast, snack, or even dinner option.
Ingredients: The batter is made from rice and urad dal, soaked, ground, and fermented overnight. This fermentation gives dosa its slight tang and airy crispness.
Texture & Flavor: Dosa is thin, golden-brown, and crispy on the outside, with a soft center. Its flavor is mildly savory with a hint of sourness from fermentation.

Serving Style: Traditionally served hot with coconut chutney, tomato chutney, and sambar. Variations include masala dosa (stuffed with spiced potato filling), rava dosa (made with semolina), paneer dosa, and many more.

title: Bonda
detailDescription: Bonda is a deep-fried South Indian snack, usually round in shape, with a crisp golden exterior and a soft, flavorful filling inside.
details: Origin & History: Bonda has roots in South India, with references dating back to the 12th century in the Sanskrit text Manasollasa. It has since evolved into many regional forms.

Ingredients: The classic Aloo Bonda is made with a spiced mashed potato filling, dipped in gram flour batter, and deep-fried until crisp. Other variations use sweet potato, tapioca, paneer, peas, or even pineapple.
Serving Style: Typically served hot with coconut chutney, tomato chutney, or sambar. In Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, it’s a favorite tea-time snack.
Texture & Flavor: Crispy outside, soft inside, with a balance of spice and comfort.

title: Bajji
detailDescription: Bajji is a popular South Indian fritter made by dipping sliced vegetables in a spiced gram flour batter and deep-frying until golden and crispy.
details: It’s a beloved street food and tea-time snack, often served hot with chutneys or ketchup.
Bajji is typically made with onions, potatoes, raw bananas, eggplant, or green chilies.
The vegetables are sliced, dipped in a batter of gram flour (besan), rice flour, chili powder, turmeric, and salt.
They are fried until crisp outside and soft inside, giving a perfect balance of crunch and flavor.
Bajji pairs wonderfully with coconut chutney, mint chutney, or simply a cup of hot chai.

Regional Variations: Bajji is known by different names across India — onion bhaji in Maharashtra, bhajia in Gujarat, and pakora in North India. Despite the variations, the essence remains the same: crispy fritters made from gram flour batter.

title: Medu Vada
description: A golden lentil doughnut with a crisp outside and soft center.
detailDescription: Medu vada is a savory South Indian fritter made from ground urad dal, shaped into a ring, and fried until golden.
details: Crisp on the outside and soft in the center.
Traditionally seasoned with curry leaves, pepper, and green chili.
Served hot with coconut chutney and sambar.

title: Masala Vada
description: A crunchy chana dal patty seasoned with aromatic spices.
detailDescription: Masala vada is a crunchy South Indian lentil fritter made with coarsely ground chana dal and aromatic spices.
details: A crisp, flat patty with a hearty lentil texture.
Seasoned with onion, curry leaves, ginger, and green chili.
Enjoyed hot as a tea-time snack or alongside chutney.

title: Puri
detailDescription: Puri is a traditional Indian deep-fried bread made from unleavened wheat flour dough, rolled into small discs and fried until it puffs up.
details: Preparation: The dough is made from whole wheat flour, water, and a pinch of salt. It’s rolled into small circles and deep-fried in hot oil until it puffs up and turns golden brown.
A staple breakfast or festive dish in Indian cuisine, puri is served hot and pairs with curries, vegetables, or sweets.
Symbol of celebration and hospitality, puri often appears at weddings, festivals, and family gatherings.
Light, airy, and golden brown, with a crisp exterior and soft interior.
Serving Tip: Enjoy hot, straight from the pan for maximum fluffiness. Symbol of warmth and hospitality in Indian households.
